control_instruction: Warm and conspiratorial, painting the room detail by detail, saving a small grin for the bouncy castle.
target_text: Imagine a birthday party. The girl is six. There are forty people in the room, and thirty of them are her parents, her grandparents, and the grandparents of her grandparents. The oldest guest is a hundred and twenty-six. He is not the one in the wheelchair. He's the one on the bouncy castle.

control_instruction: Leaning in with a knowing half-smile, then dropping to a hush on 'nobody leaves', and teasing the last line like a secret you'll keep till the end.
target_text: This is what the world looks like when humans live to one hundred and fifty. And no, it isn't a world of very old people. It's a world where nobody leaves. By the end, you'll see why, in this world, the healthiest mother on the street is her children's biggest problem.

control_instruction: Soft and almost offhand, like describing an ordinary Tuesday, the candles blown out without fuss.
target_text: It starts quietly. One morning, ageing slows down, for everyone, from wherever their body already is. A man blows out forty candles, same as last year.

control_instruction: Gathering quiet wonder, each age a small step up, and holding a breath of awe on the baby who'll see one hundred and fifty.
target_text: He'll now make it to about a hundred and thirty. His father, who's seventy, gets twenty-odd bonus years. And the baby born in the hospital across town that morning? She's the first human who will ever see one hundred and fifty.

control_instruction: Dry and matter-of-fact, then a tiny drop in pitch as every cell turns red.
target_text: Across town, at a pension company, someone changes one number on a spreadsheet. Eighty becomes one hundred and fifty. Every cell below it turns red.

control_instruction: Slowing right down, intimate, like pointing out something that was in plain sight all along.
target_text: Because here's the thing we never notice. The whole world is built around people leaving.

control_instruction: Easy and rhythmic, ticking through life's handovers like a well-worn routine, landing gently on 'moves the queue'.
target_text: You work for about forty years, then you stop. Your parents pass away, and in your fifties, you get the house. The boss retires, and somebody gets promoted. Every few decades, the jobs, the homes, the money and the power all come free again. Death is the thing that moves the queue.

control_instruction: A beat of stillness on 'the queue stops moving', then brightening into curiosity for the family photo.
target_text: Take that away, and the queue stops moving. And the first place you notice is the family photo.

control_instruction: Fond and amused, like flipping through an album, the rows piling up with comic patience.
target_text: Today, a big family photo has three rows. Grandparents at the back, parents in the middle, kids on the floor. In this world, you retake it every twenty years, and every time, the frame gets wider. By the time that baby from the hospital is a great-great-grandmother, it's five rows deep. Five generations, all alive, all healthy, all arguing about where to sit.

control_instruction: A small, pointed pause before 'almost empty', letting the image do the work.
target_text: And look at the front row. It's almost empty.

control_instruction: Clear and brisk, walking through the sums without weight, the numbers simply falling into place.
target_text: If everyone lives twice as long and keeps having kids at today's pace, the planet runs out of room. So families shrink. The world grows to about nineteen billion people, roughly double today, and then it stops. Children go from one in every four people to one in eight.

control_instruction: Tender and faintly wry, the rare child quietly outnumbered at her own party.
target_text: A kid in this world is rare. She is outnumbered by her own ancestors at her own birthday party.

control_instruction: Picking up a playful rhythm, letting 'agree on a thermostat' land with deadpan timing.
target_text: And if the family photo gets longer, so does the marriage in the middle of it. Today, "till death do us part" means about fifty years. Here, marry at thirty, and death is a hundred and twenty years away. That's a very long time to agree on a thermostat.

control_instruction: Delighted and gossipy, savouring the jeweller's rings and the first husband's speech.
target_text: So the vows change. Couples start writing an end date into them. At the jeweller's, wedding rings come engraved with a year, the way milk comes with a date. And Grandma's third wedding is a lovely day. Her first husband gives a speech.

control_instruction: Turning on a dime, crisp and a shade firmer, the fun draining out of 'aren't'.
target_text: Longer marriages are a choice. Longer careers aren't.

control_instruction: Steady and plain, laying out the arithmetic like someone who's checked it twice.
target_text: Today, you start work at twenty, stop at sixty-five, and have about fifteen years left. Here, stopping at sixty-five would leave you eighty-five years with no pay. Nobody can save for that. So the retirement age has to move, and once you do the sums, it lands at about one hundred and twenty.

control_instruction: A wry little lift on 'ninety-four', as if reading it off the payslip in disbelief.
target_text: Picture your first payslip at twenty. Near the bottom, a new line: years to retirement, ninety-four.

control_instruction: Brisk and practical, then warming with gentle amusement as the lecture hall comes into view.
target_text: But a hundred-year career has a problem. Whatever you learned at twenty is useless by sixty. So people go back to school, again and again. In a lecture hall, a seventy-year-old sits next to an eighteen-year-old.

control_instruction: Clipped and rhythmic on 'same course, same exam', then a dry smile on the eleven-page CV.
target_text: Same course. Same exam. The seventy-year-old has fifty more years of work ahead. The eighteen-year-old has a hundred. The seventy-year-old's CV is eleven pages long.

control_instruction: Thoughtful and a touch skeptical, the hopeful idea deflating page by page like the shrinking rate.
target_text: And a hundred years of work means a hundred years of paying for a home. You'd think time would make everyone rich. Give your savings a century and a half to grow, and a small pot becomes a fortune. But everyone has the same idea, all at once. Open a savings book in this world and watch the rate on each new page. It keeps getting smaller.

control_instruction: Light and knowing, a conspiratorial pause before 'It isn't.'
target_text: So people borrow instead, and the banks invent the hundred-year mortgage. It sounds cheap. It isn't.

control_instruction: Patient and precise, then a flat, deadpan landing on renting from the bank for the rest of your very long life.
target_text: On a three hundred thousand dollar house, the monthly payment drops by less than three hundred dollars. But you pay three and a half times as much interest. You're not really paying off the house. You're renting it from the bank, for the rest of your very long life.

control_instruction: Neutral as a form letter, reading the number exactly as it's printed.
target_text: A letter arrives. Payment eight hundred and forty-seven of one thousand, two hundred.

control_instruction: A quiet turn, lowering slightly on 'the one you inherit'.
target_text: Which is why everyone is waiting for the other way to get a house. The one you inherit.

control_instruction: Slow and deliberate, letting the gap from fifty to one hundred and twenty stretch out.
target_text: Today, you get your parents' home in your fifties. Here, your parents live to one hundred and fifty. They're thirty years older than you. So you get the house at one hundred and twenty. Picture the queue for one house: every heir waiting for someone to die, stretching down the street and round the block.

control_instruction: Unhurried, like a camera pushing gently along a sleepy street.
target_text: Walk down Marrow Street. Forty houses. Each front door is painted with the year it was bought.

control_instruction: Steady and observational, a dry note of resignation creeping into the comparison.
target_text: Not one of them has changed hands in ninety years. Today, about one home in forty-five comes free each year when somebody dies. Here, it's one in a hundred and fifteen. And there are twice as many people who need one.

control_instruction: Hushed and careful, almost tender over the key and its single name.
target_text: A brass key hangs inside one of those doors. It has a paper tag, for writing each owner's name. It's had one name on it for a very long time.

control_instruction: Sly and a little dark, relishing 'clever', with a deadpan sting on the birthday card.
target_text: So the young do something clever, and a little bit dark. At twenty-five, they sell their future inheritance to a bank, for cash today. The bank now owns the right to Mum's house. And every year, on Mum's birthday, the bank sends her a card. It asks how she's feeling.

control_instruction: A shade more tension, clean and observational, the brass nameplates frozen in place.
target_text: The same queue that blocks the front door blocks the top floor. On the fortieth floor of the Greyfield Exchange, the desk nameplates are engraved in brass. Nobody prints them anymore. Nobody has moved desks in eighty years.

control_instruction: Crisp and matter-of-fact, the numbers stacking up like a closing door.
target_text: Today, a top boss keeps the job for about seven years. Here, the same boss can stay for forty. Take five hundred of the biggest jobs in a country. Today, about seventy of them open up every year. Here, it's about twelve.

control_instruction: Patient and quietly comic, the man's long wait told with sympathy, the question delivered simply.
target_text: Outside one corner office, a man in a sharp suit sits on a bench. He's ninety-one. He's been waiting for this job since he was fifty. Every ten years, he asks the same thing. "Is he in?" He's in.

control_instruction: Cool and measured, a faint smile on six portraits of the same greying judge.
target_text: The same goes for judges, for professors, for anyone who holds a seat until they choose to leave. In a courthouse hallway, six portraits hang side by side. It's the same judge. Each one is a little greyer.

control_instruction: Rising with restless energy, the young building their own way out, ending on a firm 'on everything'.
target_text: So ambition leaves. If you can't climb the old ladder, you build a new one. Every founder is under forty, because only a brand new company has no queue. And the one thing young people vote for, over and over, is term limits. On everything.

control_instruction: Generous and warm, genuinely admiring the surgeon and the teacher, fair to the good side.
target_text: Now, to be fair, some of this is wonderful. A surgeon with ninety years of practice. A teacher who taught your grandmother, and now teaches you, and still remembers what your grandmother was like at your age. Longer lives have always made the world richer. That part is true.

control_instruction: Warmth fading into caution, a slow drop on 'upside down'.
target_text: But only if the old let go. And that's where it turns upside down.

control_instruction: Lightly, almost sweetly, letting 'never better' sound cheerful on its surface.
target_text: Remember the bank's birthday card? Every year it asks Mum how she's feeling. And every year, she writes back: never better.

control_instruction: The smile gone, quiet and heavy, each word placed with care, saying the thing nobody wants to say.
target_text: [sigh] Every one of those cards is another year her children rent. In this world, your parents' long, happy, healthy life is your single biggest bill. It's the one thing nobody says out loud at the birthday party.

control_instruction: A reset, calm and grounded, a small note of intrigue on 'changes shape'.
target_text: And then there's death itself. It doesn't vanish. It changes shape.

control_instruction: Gentle and matter-of-fact, a hint of affection for knees handing in their notice.
target_text: You still get old. It just starts around one hundred and thirteen. Your knees hand in their notice. You slow down for your last thirty-odd years, instead of your last fifteen.

control_instruction: Serious and steady, the numbers carrying real weight, then a dry beat on 'Because they do.'
target_text: But the biggest killer isn't age anymore. It's the road. A car crash at forty used to cost forty years. Now it costs one hundred and ten. People start driving like they have a lot to lose. Because they do.

control_instruction: Softly observant, turning the chimney-and-playground list into a quiet rhythm.
target_text: St Aldric's crematorium only needs half its building now. The other half becomes a nursery. One chimney. One playground. One car park.

control_instruction: Deadpan and gentle, letting the absurdity of the apprentice land on its own.
target_text: And the undertaker's apprentice has been training for sixty years. He's never actually seen a body.

control_instruction: Slowing into memory, warm and hushed, then tender stillness on her mother's peaceful death.
target_text: Remember the girl at the birthday party? She's one hundred and twenty now. She has a job, a mortgage, and a son who's ninety. This morning, her mother died, peacefully, in the garden, at one hundred and fifty.

control_instruction: Barely above a murmur, unhurried, every action small and deliberate, the second name written with care.
target_text: She walks up to a door on Marrow Street. The brass key is still hanging inside. Under her mother's name, on a tag that has waited a hundred and fifteen years, she writes a second one. Her own.

control_instruction: Reflective and unhurried, the ladder described with a hint of fondness for the idea.
target_text: We like to think a life is a ladder. You start at the bottom, you climb, you reach the top.

control_instruction: Quiet finality, resolute and still, letting 'death' close the video without melodrama.
target_text: It was always a queue. And the only thing that ever moved it was death.
